title: Adiabatic preparation of a fractional quantum Hall fluid by coherently pumping atoms from a Bose-Einstein condensate
authors: Alberto Tabarelli de Fatis, Christof Weitenberg, Alexander Schnell, André Eckardt, Iacopo Carusotto
abstract: We propose a protocol to adiabatically prepare a many-particle fractional quantum Hall fluid of bosonic ultracold atoms exploiting a time-dependent coherent coupling of a strongly interacting atomic state with a large dilute Bose-Einstein condensate. Starting from an empty cloud, atoms with well-defined angular momentum are coherently pumped into the fluid by Raman beams with a Laguerre-Gauss profile. Compared to number-conserving schemes which rely on finite-size-induced topological gaps, we identify an adiabatic path in the Fock space which avoids crossing topological phase transitions and thus maintains a sizable adiabatic gap open at all times. The efficiency of our preparation protocol is numerically assessed for typical experimental parameters up to particle numbers that largely exceed the experimental state-of-the-art. The crucial advantage of including an anharmonic confinement is finally highlighted.
summary: The paper proposes an advanced adiabatic protocol to create fractional quantum Hall fluids using bosonic atoms coupled to a BEC reservoir. By coherently pumping atoms while carefully controlling external parameters, the method avoids crossing detrimental topological phase transitions. This offers a robust and scalable pathway for generating highly correlated quantum matter states in cold atom experiments.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop an adiabatic protocol for preparing a many-particle fractional quantum Hall (FQH) fluid using bosonic ultracold atoms.
main_result: The proposed one-shot adiabatic ramping scheme successfully generates the target Laughlin state with high fidelity by avoiding topological phase transitions, outperforming sequential ramp methods.
method: The protocol involves adiabatically varying external pump parameters ($\Delta(t)$ and $F(t)$) to coherently transfer atoms from a Bose-Einstein condensate reservoir into the FQH system while maintaining an open adiabatic gap.
model_or_system: The system consists of bosonic ultracold atoms in two states: one forming the FQH fluid (in the Lowest Landau Level, LLL) and the other acting as a BEC reservoir. The dynamics are governed by a time-dependent Hamiltonian incorporating coupling terms ($\hat{H}_P(t)$).
key_observables: Fidelity ($1-F$), adiabatic gap size, occupation of particle number sectors ($N$).
important_parameters: The magnetic length ($l_B$), the ratio of BEC sound velocity to FQH atom speed ($c_{	ext{BEC}} / v_{	ext{FQH}}$), and the maximum pump strength ($F_{max}$).
main_assumptions: The LLL approximation is used, and in later analyses, phonon emission from FQH atoms into the BEC must be suppressed.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the coupling scheme (Fig. 1), the many-body spectrum showing Laughlin states (Fig. 2a), the adiabatic evolution path (Fig. 3), and comparisons of fidelity between one-shot vs. sequential ramps (Fig. 7).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical model, details the Hamiltonian in the LLL manifold, proposes the adiabatic pumping protocol by controlling time-dependent parameters ($\Delta(t)$, $F(t)$), and numerically assesses the fidelity and gap protection across various ramp profiles.
why_interesting: This work provides a detailed theoretical roadmap for realizing exotic topological quantum states (FQH) using highly controllable ultracold atomic platforms, directly addressing challenges in adiabatic state preparation.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Proposed scheme for the generation of an FQH fluid of ultracold atoms. The FQH system under study is formed of atoms in a strongly interacting state |2⟩close to a Fesh- bach resonance (see End Matter), tightly trapped in a two- dimensional geometry; in the frame rotating at frequency Ω, the atoms experience an effective synthetic magnetic field. This FQH system is coherently coupled via two Raman beams with a Laguerre-Gauss profile to a weakly interacting conden- sate |1⟩that acts as a particle reservoir, exchanging an angular momentum l per particle. The FQH is initially empty, and is adiabatically pumped to the desired state in a time T.

FIG. 2. (a) Many-body spectrum of the system in the LLL manifold as a function of the total angular momentum, in the case of no external potential in the rotating frame. Different colors refer to different number sectors. Red dots denote the Laughlin states, of angular momentum L = N(N−1), and the blue square is the state with one quasi-hole and N = 4. The arrows indicate the transitions coupling the vacuum to the N = 4 Laughlin state, using a pump with angular momentum l = 3. Transitions to larger N are suppressed by the many- body gap. (b) Many-body gap above the Laughlin state as a function of N for g/l2 B = 3.77ℏΩ.

FIG. 3. (a) Instantaneous eigenstates during the adiabatic evolution with F = 0 (dashed lines) and first two eigenstates for F(t) ̸= 0 (solid lines). (b) Sketch of the temporal ramp of the pump strength F(t) and the detuning ∆(t). (c) Illustra- tion of the adiabatic scheme as the tunneling in a tilted lattice comprising the states coupled by the pump F: initially, the system is in the N = 0 vacuum state; at the end, it is frozen in the Nt = 4 Laughlin state protected by the many-body gap (blue dot).

FIG. 4. Infidelity with Nt = 4 Laughlin state for different initial and final detuning, for a C∞ramp of ramp time T = 127TΩ (318 ms), for (a) Fmax/Ω= 0.05, (b) 0.1, (c) 0.2. The dashed line marks the many-body gap. (d) Infidelity with the Nt = 7 Laughlin state for ramps with different smoothness, as a function of time, rescaled by the sharpness of ∆(s = t/T). (e) Ramp time T required to reach a desired fidelity as a function of Nt, for a C0 ramp with ∆f = −∆0 = 0.1Ωand Fmax = 0.1Ω. The solid lines refer to a purely harmonic potential, whereas dashed lines include a quartic potential with V0 = 0.001ℏΩ. The detunings include the energy shift due to the quartic potential.
